latest_final: After a deliberate murder of their romantic partner, the speaker sets out to cover it up by producing a forged farewell note in the dead partner's own voice — a message addressed to themselves reading "You've disappointed me so much; I'm never coming back." The note's job is to make the partner's absence look voluntary: everyone should conclude the partner dumped the speaker and walked away, so no one treats the disappearance as a crime. To make the forgery convincing, the speaker rehearses it — writing the same line again and again, so the repeated sentence appears seven times as their practice attempts at the fake goodbye. With a believable note in hand, the cover story becomes "they left me and are never coming back." The closing "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble" is a wry, flat understatement: the speaker knows they are now a murderer, and knows the whole deception may come apart. The core twist is that the seemingly sorrowful breakup line, repeated seven times, is not a parting message from a lover at all — it is a killer grinding out a forgery to explain away the partner they deliberately killed, and the "disappointment" is the murderer's own rehearsed fiction.
